(The Center Square) – Trump-endorsed incumbent U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles lost a primary challenge to Charlie Hatcher, a former Tennessee agriculture commissioner, in a Republican contest marked by new congressional districts approved in May.
Tennessee Sen. Brent Taylor and Rep. Justin Pearson are also set to face off in Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District, the first general election in its new reconfiguration.
Rep. Steve Cohen, D-Tenn., decided not to run for reelection after his Memphis district was divided by the General Assembly to give Republicans an edge in congressional races and all nine of Tennessee's seats.
Here is a look at the results from the newly-drawn districts.
District 5
Chaz Molder secured the Democratic Party's nomination and will face Hatcher in November.
Ogles, who was endorsed by Trump, came under fire for controversial social media statements over the past several months. He was also investigated by the Justice Department over improper campaign finance allegations. The department seized his personal cellphone as part of the investigation, according to a previous report from The Center Square.
“Muslims don’t belong in America. Pluralism is a lie,” Ogles posted to social media in March. Additionally, Ogles' social media account had a post that said, “Homosexuality has no place in America." The post was deleted and Ogles blamed a staff member.
Hatcher focused his campaign on supporting Trump and pushing for stronger agricultural policy. Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee went against Trump’s endorsement to vouch for Hatcher.
“Charlie Hatcher and I have been friends for 25 years," Lee said in a video. “For seven years, he served as my commissioner of agriculture. I know Charlie. I know his conservative values and how much he loves our country.”
Hatcher raised concerns about foreign ownership of farms in the United States. He said U.S. adversaries are seeking to gain intellectual property information from agricultural purchases in the state.
“Food security is national security and food is power,” Hatcher said. “It’d be my intention to protect American and Tennessee agriculture because it is the best agriculture on the globe. And we’re under threat from our adversaries.”
Hatcher also appeared to criticize Ogles for his rhetoric.
"Think about what President Trump could do if our congressman spent less time talking and more time doing," Hatcher's website reads.
Ogles is the ninth incumbent House member to lose a primary ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Three Republicans and six Democrats have lost their primaries.
Molder, the mayor of Columbia since 2018, has touted his legislative record of passing balanced budgets without property tax increases. He called for expanding healthcare coverage, lowering prescription drug costs and funding rural hospitals
“Protecting these vital healthcare resources is essential to improving health outcomes for all residents,” Molder’s website reads.
District 9
Pearson, 31, was first elected to the Tennessee House of Representatives in 2023 after first serving in an acting capacity. Taylor quickly jumped into the race after the Tennessee legislature announced its new district maps.
Pearson defeated M. LaTroy A-Williams and state Sen. London Lamar.
Taylor beat Tennessee Rep. Todd Warner and Jeremy Thompson in the Republican primary.
Taylor, who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, has called for supporting the president’s agenda and building a coalition to avoid impeachment.
“If we want strong borders, and we want to end illegal immigration, and we want to support President Trump and his laying out and implementing his agenda, and we want to provide impeachment insurance for President Trump in these final two years in office, we have to win,” Taylor said.
Pearson received an influx of support from prominent Democrats across the country. He has focused his campaign on increasing the minimum wage, doubling the earned income tax credit and supporting a guaranteed basic income for people who lost their jobs.
He has strongly advocated against building AI data centers in Memphis, an area that has seen an increased presence of the technology's development.
“I’m running for Congress to help lead that fight and hold billionaires like Elon Musk and giant corporations accountable for the damage AI is doing to our communities,” Pearson said.
District 8
Tennessee’s eighth congressional district was also affected by the state’s redistricting effort, as it took on greater portions of Memphis from the ninth district. Rep. David Kustoff, R-Tenn., will face off against Heidi Kuhn to represent the newly drawn district in November.
Kuhn defeated Dewey Gordon Bryan and Leonard Perkins for the party's nomination. Kustoff ran unopposed.
Kustoff, who was endorsed by Trump, has touted his tough stance on crime, his service as U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Tennessee, and his dismantling of tax mandates for individuals without healthcare.
“You are no longer forced by the government to buy insurance you don’t want or need,” Kustoff’s website reads. “I will continue to work to dismantle Obamacare once and for all so we can offer the best healthcare in the world.”
Kuhn, a criminal court clerk, said she is focused on expanding child tax credits, low-income housing credits and repealing cuts to SNAP made over the last year by the Trump administration.
“We deserve a future where families can afford to buy a home—not just get by,” Kuhn said. “I’m running for Congress to fight for lower costs and more opportunity for West Tennessee.”

Trump-backed Andy Ogles loses reelection bid and other Tennessee primary results
By David Wright, Katie Doran, CNN
(CNN) — Former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher defeated conservative firebrand Rep. Andy Ogles on Thursday in the Republican primary in the state’s newly redrawn 5th District, in the latest loss for a Trump-backed candidate.
Hatcher will face Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, who won the Democratic primary, in November.
While President Donald Trump’s endorsement has proven decisive in many Republican primaries this year, he’s also seen some notable defeats. In governor’s races in Iowa and Georgia, Randy Feenstra and Lt. Gov. Burt Jones fell short in their bids, while Trump issued a dual endorsement in South Carolina after his initial pick, Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette, failed to avoid a runoff and ultimately lost.
Ogles’ defeat comes just days after Michigan Republicans spurned the president’s recommendation in a House race – backing Tom Smith, a little known candidate who dropped out of the primary in July, over Trump-backed Amir Hassan.
“Last night was another good night for Endorsements, 8-1, and the 1 was a person who I remained loyal to even though he had virtually no chance of winning,” Trump posted Friday on Truth Social, referencing Ogles. He gave Hatcher his “Complete and Total Endorsement!”
Several key races were on the ballot in Tennessee Thursday, as voters cast their first ballots under a new Republican-drawn congressional map aimed at delivering the GOP a clean sweep of the state’s nine districts.
Trump saw success in the redrawn 9th District, where his chosen candidate, GOP state Sen. Brent Taylor, will take on Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson, after Republican lawmakers pushed through a new congressional map earlier this year that split the current Memphis-based seat into three separate districts that favor the GOP.
Thursday’s primaries also set the general election matchup in the race for governor in deep-red Tennessee, although Trump stayed on the sidelines of the Republican contest. CNN projects that GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn will face Democratic Memphis City Councilmember Jerri Green in the fall – a guarantee that Tennessee’s next governor will be the first woman to hold the role.
See the results below:
Another Trump-backed candidate loses
Ogles, a member of the far-right House Freedom Caucus, is a staunch Trump ally but has frequently been at the center of controversy during his time in Congress.
Most recently, Republican and Democratic lawmakers in June condemned a now-deleted post on Ogles’ X account that said, “Homosexuality has no place in America,” which the congressman blamed on a staffer. But Ogles has stood by similar remarks declaring what the country should look like, writing in March on X that “Muslims don’t belong in American society.”
He has also been the subject of a congressional ethics inquiry into whether he violated campaign finance laws.
Hatcher, however, was bolstered by his strong political ties in the state – including an endorsement from GOP Gov. Bill Lee in the final days of the primary. Hatcher promised to support Trump if elected, which the president noted in his Truth Social post, calling Hatcher a “Great ‘Trump’ Candidate.”
A fifth-generation dairy farmer, Hatcher pledges to work to support farmers, protect American food security, reduce energy costs and improve public infrastructure if elected in November.
Since it was redrawn in May amid a wave of mid-cycle redistricting, Tennessee’s 5th District takes on a long, skinny shape snaking up from Memphis to the Kentucky border and down again to part of Williamson County. It includes parts of 17 counties.
The new district lines are more advantageous to Republicans, giving Hatcher an edge heading into November.
Ogles’ loss complicates Democrats’ path
Heading into Thursday, Democrats were hopeful that a favorable national political environment along with a strong potential candidate in Molder and a series of controversies swirling around Ogles could potentially put the seat in play.
Hatcher’s win may change those calculations.
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee offered early support to Molder, who was was first elected mayor in 2018 when he defeated a two-term incumbent Republican, including him in its “Red to Blue” program for strong recruits.
While redistricting upended the race this spring, Molder decided to continue his run, centering his campaign on issues like lowering the cost of living, expanding healthcare access and making housing more affordable.
He defeated four other candidates to secure the Democratic nomination. Molder far out-raised other candidates in both parties vying for the 5th District, bringing in $2.6 million by mid-July, according to Federal Election Commission filings.
A member of the ‘Tennessee Three’ faces stiff odds in redrawn district
The 9th District race serves as a case study in mid-decade redistricting and how quickly it can transform electoral dynamics.
As part of a national wave of partisan redistricting kicked off by Texas Republicans last summer, GOP state lawmakers approved a new congressional map in May, breaking up the Black-majority district centered on Memphis, the state’s lone Democratic seat, to favor Republicans. The move prompted US Rep. Steve Cohen, who has held the seat for nearly 20 years, to announce he would not seek reelection.
Pearson, who defeated state Sen. London Lamar in the primary, gained national prominence in 2023 as one of three Tennessee lawmakers who Republicans in the state legislature moved to expel following a gun control protest. He was expelled from the legislature but ultimately reinstated.
He now advances to a general election facing stiff odds in the new 9th District, as Democrats hope to overcome the transformed political landscape.
Pearson will face Taylor, a fellow state legislator who has aligned himself closely with President Donald Trump, describing his campaign as “ironclad impeachment insurance.”
Taylor’s bid was bolstered by Trump’s support and that of Tennessee’s two Republican senators, Blackburn and Bill Hagerty.
Blackburn defeats Rose
Blackburn’s win Thursday positions her to become the first female governor of the reliably red state.
Blackburn, who has represented Tennessee in the state legislature and US Congress since the 1990s, defeated Rep. John Rose and state Rep. Monty Fritts. She entered the race as a heavy favorite to succeed GOP Gov. Bill Lee, who is term-limited, but she faced unexpected pressure in its home stretch.
With President Donald Trump declining to endorse in the race, Blackburn touted her support for his agenda. She took flak from Rose, however, over her vote to certify former President Joe Biden’s 2020 electoral victory and her refusal to debate.
Despite the headwinds, Blackburn prevailed and looks set to add to her lengthy resume in Tennessee politics, advancing to a general election where she’s favored to hold the governor’s office for Republicans.
Democrats select a nominee for governor
In a state that President Donald Trump won by almost 30 points in 2024, Green will likely face a steep uphill battle against Blackburn.
She campaigned on ending Tennessee’s grocery tax, increasing funding for public schools and eliminating medical debt for thousands of people.
Green began her career as a juvenile public defender and currently serves as Shelby County’s interim chief public defender, a role she took on at the start of 2026. On public safety, Green has emphasized a rehabilitative approach to justice and the importance of ensuring fair courtroom representation.
Seen as the front-runner throughout the primary, Green defeated activist Carnita Atwater and pastor Kevin Lee McCants to secure the party nomination.

sources.news_title: Rep. Andy Ogles loses Republican primary in Tennessee
sources.text:
Rep. Andy Ogles loses Republican primary in Tennessee
Published in Political News
Tennessee Rep. Andy Ogles lost his primary Thursday, becoming the third House Republican to lose a renomination bid this year.
Ogles was trailing former state Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher, 53% to 47%, when The Associated Press called the race for the 5th District at 10:10 p.m. Thursday.
The result represents a rare defeat for President Donald Trump, who had reiterated his support for Ogles earlier Thursday, saying on social media that the second-term congressman was doing a “fantastic job.” It’s the second loss this week for a Trump-endorsed Republican, after Navy veteran Amir Hassan came up short in a House primary in Michigan.
Other House Republicans who’ve lost primary challenges this year include Reps. Daniel Crenshaw of Texas and Thomas Massie of Kentucky, while six Democratic incumbents have so far been defeated in their House primaries.
Ogles has been dogged by controversy since he was first elected to Congress in 2022. He’s been accused of embellishing his résumé and is under a House Ethics investigation into his campaign finances. And he drew criticism this year for saying that Muslims “don’t belong in American society” and that “homosexuality has no place in America.”
Ogles was also running in a district that was considerably altered under Tennessee’s new congressional map. Once based in Middle Tennessee, the 5th District now snakes along the Kentucky border, connecting Memphis to the Nashville area. State Republicans redrew the map to help them win all nine of the state’s House seats, but Ogles ended up with a district with mostly new constituents.
Hatcher, who emphasized his background as a dairy farmer and veterinarian, won a late endorsement this week from Gov. Bill Lee, adding to support from former Gov. Bill Haslam. And while Hatcher didn’t have Trump’s backing in the primary, he has praised the president and vowed to support his agenda in Congress. Hatcher also outraised Ogles, bringing in $720,000 to his $613,000 through July 17.
Hatcher benefited from $2 million in outside support from the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition PAC, a group backed by clean energy investors that ran ads portraying Ogles as a showhorse and casting Hatcher as a worker.
The Freedom Caucus Fund, meanwhile, spent $780,000 to boost Ogles on the air.
Hatcher will next face Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, who won a five-way primary for the Democratic nomination Thursday. Molder is the fundraising leader in the race, hauling in $2.6 million through July 17, with $1.5 million in the bank.
Democrats still see Molder as a strong candidate, despite the redrawn district lines. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added the seat to its target list last year and included him in its Red to Blue program. But the new version of the 5th District even redder under the new map, transforming from a seat Trump won by 18 points in 2024 to one he would have carried by 23 points.
Other races
Tennessee Sen. Marsha Blackburn prevailed in a three-way Republican primary Thursday in the race to succeed the term-limited Lee.
With 90% of the vote in, Blackburn had 43% of the vote to 33% for Rep. John W. Rose and 23% for state Rep. Monty Fritts, the AP reported.
The Volunteer State is now guaranteed to elect its first female governor, with Blackburn strongly favored to defeat Memphis City Councilwoman Jeri Green, who won the Democratic nomination Thursday.
Blackburn’s Senate colleague, Republican Bill Hagerty, was unopposed in his primary Thursday and advanced to a rematch from six years ago against Democratic environmentalist Marquita Bradshaw.
Meanwhile, two Republicans are likely heading to the House next year after winning primaries for deep-red open seats.
In the race to succeed Rose in the 6th District, state Rep. Johnny Garrett won the GOP nomination, defeating former Rep. Van Hilleary and two other candidates. Hilleary, who was previously Rose’s chief of staff, was seeking a comeback to the House after serving four terms from 1995 to 2003.
And in the 9th District, state Sen. Brent Taylor, who was endorsed by Trump, won a four-way GOP primary for the redrawn seat.
The 9th has long been a Democratic bastion anchored in Memphis, but under the new map, it now stretches from Memphis to the Nashville area along the state’s border with Mississippi and Alabama and would have backed Trump by 21 points in 2024, according to Inside Elections.

Ogles was also running in a district that was considerably altered under Tennessee’s new congressional map. Former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher has defeated incumbent U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles in the Republican primary for Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District on Aug. 6, overcoming the controversial congressman's endorsement from President Donald Trump.
He will face Democratic Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder in the general election, who topped a five-candidate field including Memphis City Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton.
“Apparently, 'Hire a farmer' resonated with the constituents of the 5th District,” Hatcher said to a cheering crowd at his Franklin watch party. “I'm going to carry that work ethic, that ability to get the job done, to solve problems as veterinarians or farmers do every day, and to serve others.”
Hatcher was endorsed by Gov. Bill Lee two days before the primary.
In a statement to social media, Molder thanked his volunteers and voters.
"Tonight, we took a huge step forward in our journey toward dignified, responsive leadership for Tennessee's 5th District," Molder wrote. In a follow-up post, he wrote, "The next few months will be busy. We're committed to showing up in all 17 counties across #TN5, listening, learning, and earning your trust every step of the way."
Unofficial results provided by the Tennessee Secretary of State's Office.
Ogles was met with applause as he walked into his watch party at The Grecian Family Restaurant and Bakery in Spring Hill around 9:15 p.m. He said he had called his opponent to congratulate him.
"Nobody likes to lose, but the results are in and, look, we've fought a great race," Ogles said.
Ogles said he offered to help Hatcher if he takes office.
"It has been an absolute honor to serve Tennessee as a member of Congress, and I look forward to helping Charlie as he transitions and then helping any of you throughout the remainder of my term," Ogles said.
At Hatcher's watch party earlier in the night, Maddie Hobaica, 21, a student at Lipscomb University, said Hatcher’s background and values inspired her to put a red campaign badge over her uniform as she worked the party.
“The fact that he comes from a farmer family," Hobaica said, "that’s kind of what America is built on.”
Hatcher's family friend Jed Mangram said he had worked for Hatcher since he was about 13.
“There’s nobody, no one I'd rather trust in Congress than him," Mangram said.
An ardent supporter of President Donald Trump, two-term incumbent Ogles had become one of the more controversial Republicans in Congress this year, calling for a cessation of legal immigration and an exile of Muslims from American society. Ogles met with sanctioned Russian State Duma delegates, spoke alongside Christian nationalists and called for an FCC investigation of the Super Bowl halftime show.
Hatcher launched a well-funded challenge, earning support from Lee, former Tennessee Gov. Bill Haslam, former Trump Agriculture Secretary Sonny Perdue and former U.S. Rep. Zach Wamp. Hatcher is a fifth-generation dairy farmer, veterinarian and businessman who served as Tennessee’s agriculture commissioner for seven years and owns Hatcher Family Dairy.
Ogles has held the 5th District seat since 2022, after Republicans redrew Nashville into three congressional districts, paving the way for a Republican. He has been under scrutiny throughout his time in office over campaign finance discrepancies centered around his 2022 disclosure of a self-loan of $320,000, a sum he later admitted was never actually contributed to his campaign. His phone was confiscated by the FBI during an investigation he said he thought was related to errors in his campaign finance disclosures. The Justice Department returned Ogles' phone this year and said it would destroy investigative records.
Ogles has the lowest vote attendance rate of Tennessee’s congressional delegation and has missed more votes than almost anyone in Congress, having missed more than 8% of the scheduled votes since he was elected in 2022.
During the final days of the race, a PAC called the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition touted $2 million in spending on ads attacking Ogles. The Freedom Caucus Fund has spent nearly $485,000 backing Ogles and attacking Hatcher.
On the Democratic side of the ballot, Molder has been mayor of Columbia, located in Maury County, since 2018, when he defeated two-term incumbent Republican Mayor Dean Dickey.
How redistricting reshaped the race
Tennessee Republicans kneecapped the challengers of Trump-endorsed Ogles by drawing Hatcher's and Molder’s home bases out of the 5th District during Congressional redistricting in May.
The new 5th District loops together parts of Franklin and Clarksville with downtown Memphis and 14 other rural counties in the northwest corner of the state, and borders Kentucky, Missouri, Arkansas and Mississippi.
Incumbents typically have the advantage of name recognition. But only 17% of the district’s original constituents remained after redistricting, which somewhat leveled the playing field. While Ogles had some advantage in incumbency, Hatcher said familiarity with the farming communities built during his years as agriculture commissioner laid solid groundwork in the district’s rural counties.
“Most people say it helped me. It added several of the highest ag-revenue counties in the state of Tennessee, so when they redistricted a lot of people in the new counties, especially in West Tennessee, they don’t know Andy Ogles,” Hatcher said last month. “But if they know anybody in these ag communities, they know Charlie Hatcher.”
Driving across the district was time consuming for all the candidates. Hatcher said he put in 12- and 17-hour days several times a week to connect with voters at events in rural counties.
“The big challenge is the distance, 380 or 400 miles from Hohenwald to Fort Campbell to Lake County and down in the west,” Hatcher said.
The Trump effect?
Trump endorsed Ogles before Hatcher got into the race. When Ogles appeared to be slipping amid attacks from out-of-state groups, Trump stepped in, joining a tele-rally on July 28 hosted by the Freedom Fund. “Andy will be, really, enshrined as one of the best congressmen that you’ll ever see,” Trump said.
But his endorsement of Ogles was more aloof than in the past.
“I got to love Tennessee … I love that place. And it’s been good for me, and I’ve been good for it,” Trump said, touting his own resounding electoral wins in 2016, 2020 and 2024.
“I’m always going to love Tennessee, even if you don’t vote for Andy,” he said.
Looking to November
Trump won the areas in the new district by 23 points in 2024. But in the 2018 Senate race between Marsha Blackburn and Phil Bredesen, partisan lean in the new 5th District was even.
While the district was drawn to give Republicans a political advantage, internal polling released by Molder’s campaign last month found Molder just 6 percentage points behind Ogles, with 12% of voters undecided.
Analysts at Cook Political Report moved analysis of the 5th District from “likely R” to “solid R” after redistricting. Analysts said Ogles caught "a huge break after redistricting” as the district no longer includes Nashville or Democratic challenger Molder’s home base in the city of Columbia.
But Molder has significantly out-fundraised both Hatcher and Ogles, bringing in nearly $2 million since declaring his candidacy last year, according to Federal Election Commission data.
He's also earned endorsements from former U.S. Rep. Jim Cooper, U.S. Rep. Steve Cohen and former Tennessee Gov. Phil Bredesen. Molder has been named a priority “Red to Blue” candidate by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, a designation that comes with logistical, strategic, and fundraising support, and signals national Democrats' confidence they can flip the 5th District in November.

By DAVID A. LIEB and KRISTIN M. HALL
MEMPHIS, Tenn. (AP) — Former Tennessee Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher defeated U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles in a Republican primary Thursday for a significantly reshaped congressional district — marking a rare rejection of a candidate endorsed by President Donald Trump.
Voters also picked a pair of Memphis-area lawmakers to square off in another vastly reconfigured U.S. House district. Trump-backed state Sen. Brent Taylor will face Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson, who gained national prominence when he was expelled from the Tennessee House for protesting in support of gun control measures.
The primaries provided the first test of a new U.S. House map that was redrawn in May by Republican state lawmakers after the U.S. Supreme Court weakened federal Voting Rights Act protections for minorities. Trump cheered along the redistricting as part of a broader national plan to try to hold on to a slim House majority in the midterm elections.
Republicans already hold eight of the state’s nine congressional seats and will be going for a clean sweep of the districts in November.
The previously compact 9th Congressional District, based in Memphis, had a majority Black population and is represented by a Democrat. But it was cracked apart by Republicans this year, causing a ripple of changes that also reconfigured Ogles’ 5th District.
A Trump-endorsed candidate is defeated
Ogles, a member of the conservative Freedom Caucus, had faced controversies related to his campaign finances and resume, among other things. But Trump gave him an early endorsement last fall — and praised him on Election Day as “a Conservative Warrior” — as Ogles sought a third term in the reshaped district.
Ogles capitalized on a previous redistricting in the 2022 elections, winning a formerly Democratic-held seat that was reshaped to Republicans’ advantage by splitting the Nashville area among three districts.
The new 5th District stretches from Ogles’ base in central Tennessee to the northwest corner of the state before snaking south along the Mississippi River to Memphis — with 82% its voters new, according to an Associated Press estimate.
Although he lacked Trump’s endorsement, Hatcher was backed by Republican Gov. Bill Lee, under whom he served for seven years. Hatcher campaigned as pro-Trump while emphasizing his farming background.
“Think what President Trump could do if our congressman spent less time talking and more time doing,” Hatcher’s campaign website said.
Trump has mostly backed winners so far in this year’s Republican primaries, though his favored candidate in Michigan’s 8th Congressional District primary, Amir Hassan, lost Tuesday.
Ogles’ controversies have included the FBI seizing his cellphone in 2024 as part of an investigation into his campaign finance reporting. The Justice Department recently agreed to return the device, signaling that it was abandoning the probe, which began under the Biden administration.
In 2023, Ogles acknowledged that he had graduated with a liberal studies degree from Middle Tennessee State University, saying he was “mistaken” for previously describing it as an international relations degree.
Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder won the Democratic primary in the 5th District.
Pearson and Taylor to face off in revamped Memphis district
The new 9th District stretches about 200 miles (320 kilometers) east from Memphis across rural areas before reaching north toward Nashville. It previously favored Democrats but now tilts Republican, with 71% of voters new to the district, according to an AP estimate.
After the redistricting, longtime Democratic Rep. Steve Cohen announced that he would no longer seek reelection.
Pearson is a Memphis activist who was reelected by voters after being expelled from the state House by Republican lawmakers in 2023.
Pearson noted to supporters Thursday night that it was 61 years ago to the day that the Voting Rights Act was signed. He said the Supreme Court and Tennessee lawmakers have effectively undone portions of it, leading to the redrawing of the formerly majority-Black district.
“The political dilution and degradation of our rights is happening,” Pearson said. But he added: “We’re one step closer to Washington, D.C.”
Taylor said in a statement to supporters that “Pearson is the face of the extreme left in this race — the same activist who has repeatedly put chaos over order.”
Pearson attacked Taylor for accepting contributions from entities associated with Elon Musk.
While Pearson opposed Trump’s deployment of National Guard troops to address crime in Memphis last year, Taylor joined other Republicans in supporting it, calling it “an investment.”
Taylor also sponsored a 2024 law that required law enforcement agencies to communicate with federal immigration authorities if they discover people are in the country illegally.
Memphis voters voice their dismay over redistricting
For decades Memphis, the most populous city in Shelby County, formed the base of its own congressional district. Now the county is split among three districts that extend outward like spokes into rural areas.
Lonzo Taylor, a retired postal worker and military veteran, said Black voters like himself have had their voices diluted.
“We only had one district in the whole state of Tennessee, and you don’t even want that to be fair? It’s just terrible,” said Taylor, 72. “I love this state, but I am very disappointed in our governor,” who called lawmakers into a special session for the redistricting.
Terrice Thomas, 45, an educator who votes for Democrats, had to learn a lot more about the candidates when she got switched from District 9 to District 8. She is concerned Memphis constituents could get overlooked.
“Is everybody going to have an equal say on what’s happening in their communities or even the people that you’re voting for?” Thomas said. “Are they going to really take into account the different areas and what makes us unique?”
Garrett wins Republican primary for open seat in the 6th District
Republican U.S. Rep. John Rose opted not to seek reelection in the 6th District to run for governor instead. That created a contentious primary for the Republican-leaning district, which stretches east from Nashville.
State Rep. Johnny Garrett won a Republican primary that included Rose’s recent chief of staff, former U.S. Rep. Van Hilleary, who served eight years in Congress before losing a gubernatorial bid in 2002.
Mike Croley won a five-way Democratic primary.
Republican voters pick Blackburn for governor
U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn defeated Rose in the GOP primary to succeed Gov. Lee, who is barred by term limits from seeking reelection. Blackburn, who won her second six-year Senate term in 2024, would have to give the seat up if elected.
Memphis City Council member Jerri Green won the Democratic gubernatorial primary.
Republicans have held the governor’s office since 2011 and won every U.S. Senate election since 1994. Sen. Bill Hagerty won the Republican primary without opposition and will face Marquita Bradshaw, who won the Democratic nomination, in November.
___
The story has been updated to correct the day of the primary election to Thursday, from Tuesday.
___
Lieb reported from Jefferson City, Missouri. AP writer Geoff Mulvihill contributed from Haddonfield, New Jersey.

sources.text:
Listen to Banner reporters discuss the Aug. 6 primary election results.
U.S. Rep. Andy Ogles, a bomb-throwing Tennessee Republican, lost his bid for reelection Thursday as GOP challenger Charlie Hatcher won the Republican nomination in the redrawn 5th Congressional District.
Hatcher will face Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, who won in the Democratic primary, in the November general election.
Hatcher was until recently the Tennessee commissioner of agriculture and is the owner of Hatcher Family Dairy in College Grove. He had attracted the support of establishment Republican figures like Gov. Bill Lee, former Gov. Bill Haslam and former Trump cabinet member Sonny Perdue. It was a coalition similar to the one that backed Metro Councilmember Courtney Johnston’s failed 2024 primary challenge against Ogles.
Ogles has consistently generated controversy and scrutiny since emerging from a crowded Republican primary in 2022. He has filed incorrect and late campaign finance disclosures, misled the public about his resume and said: “Muslims don’t belong in American society.”
The Freedom Caucus Fund has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars both supporting Ogles and opposing Hatcher. The clean energy group Invest in Tomorrow Coalition has done the same on behalf of Hatcher and opposed to Ogles.
For years, the district primarily consisted of Davidson County, and was reliably won by Democrats. Ahead of the 2022 cycle, Republicans in the Tennessee legislature split Davidson County into three districts, with each favoring Republicans. The district was redrawn earlier this year again, as Tennessee Republicans sought to aid national GOP midterm efforts by splitting Memphis into three districts.
Now, the 5th District includes part of Williamson and Maury counties, then snakes northwest through rural parts of West Tennessee, then down the Mississippi River into the heart of Memphis. Hatcher narrowly beat Ogles in the latter’s home Maury County.
President Trump had endorsed Ogles and spoke at a “tele-rally” for the candidate the week prior to Thursday’s primary.
“Andy’s always been there when we needed him,” Trump said, later adding that, “even if you don’t vote for Andy, I’ve got to love Tennessee, to be honest with you.”
Molder was a prized recruit for local and national Democrats when he entered the race for the old 5th District. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the national House Democratic political organization, committed to supporting his campaign, a sign that Washington saw the seat as flippable.
When the Tennessee legislature hastily redrew the map, they barely excluded the homes of both Molder and Hatcher, who both opted to run in the district anyway. Molder saw some benefit to the changes, though, as the new district included Ripley, where his wife is from. His father-in-law, Craig Fitzhugh, is a popular former state lawmaker and current mayor of Ripley.
Molder raised more than $2.5 million prior to the primary and has kept most of that in reserves for what promises to be an uphill general election. Also in Thursday’s Democratic primary were Rachel Hurley of Memphis, DeVante Hill of Bartlett, Yolanda Cooper-Sutton of Memphis and Carrie Ann Iacomini of Memphis. Cooper-Sutton secured nearly a third of the vote, coming within a single-digit margin of Molder. She also led Molder in Lauderdale County, home to Ripley, though the county only tallied just north of 1,000 votes in the Democratic primary.
James Johnson of Memphis and Micheál O’Leary of Nashville are running as independents.
